query: For AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock intended for additively manufactured miniature components, what single intervention could overcome the residual thermal stresses, degraded mechanical properties, and processing complexity associated with mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing regimes? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to components made under conventional high-thermal-load additive-manufacturing conditions, states the applicable processing window, geometry, and test conditions, identifies supporting prior evidence, and describes a falsification experiment.

falsification_experiment.design: Comparative study of additive manufacturing of AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock using conventional high-thermal-load conditions and multi-scale modeling optimized process parameters
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the application of multi-scale modeling of additive manufacturing processes does not result in improved mechanical properties and reduced processing complexity compared to conventional high-thermal-load additive-manufacturing conditions, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Additive manufacturing (AM) is rapidly emerging as a pivotal technology for industrial part production due to its ability to create intricate shapes through computer-assisted layer-by-layer part construction. In metal AM, a broad, ever-expanding technology landscape has emerged with varying degrees of adoption in industry. While various AM technologies exist, liquid-mediated metal AM, notably Laser Powder Bed Fusion (L-PBF), has garnered significant interest in industry and academia due to its potential to produce high-quality parts. L-PBF’s quality relies on understanding the interplay between process parameters, material properties, and solidification conditions. Traditional alloy design primarily targets specific manufacturing routes and often overlooks the unique demands of additive manufacturing (AM). In AM, designing alloys requires optimizing both chemistry and processing conditions simultaneously to minimize defects and enhance reliability. Conventional approaches first focus on achieving target properties and then on developing scalable processing methods. AM is an emerging new technology by which components are manufactured in a layer-by-layer manner based on a computer-aided design (CAD) model to create a complex three-dimensional shape,. Unlike conventional manufacturing processes (casting, machining, etc.), which have shape limitations, AM has almost no geometric constraints, which allows the manufacturing of a variety of complex shapes,. Because of this characteristic, it is possible to manufacture components that were difficult to manufacture before, as well as high-performance parts for use in aerospace, defense, automotive and biomedical fields. Since the selective laser melting (SLM) process offers a fast cooling rate among the metal AM processes, it is possible to improve the mechanical properties along with achieving an excellent dimensional accuracy,. Due to these advantages, SLM is one of the most studied AM techniques at present, and SLM is expected to be the most suitable method for manufacturing HEA.

However, a process such as mechanical alloying is still required to incorporate the dispersoids into the metal matrix prior to building with AM. Furthermore, AM processing with mechanically alloyed powder is problematic because the highly deformed powders have poor flow and, thus, reduced feedstock delivery properties. Studies have also shown that powder shape and size distribution contribute significantly to the quality of AM builds. Other methods of incorporating nanoparticles into additive powder lots through chemical reactions or depositions have been explored; though the added complexity and expense of these techniques may limit their commercial viability,,. For this study, we produced AM NiCoCr mechanical test specimens with dispersed nanoscale yttrium oxides (Y2O3) that are suitable for use in high-temperature applications through a new, economically viable method. Mechanical and microstructural analysis confirm the success this new fabrication pathway had in creating dispersion strengthened metallic alloys.
